{{Short description|Opposite of Murphy's law}}
'''Yhprum's law''' is the opposite of [[Murphy's law]]. ("Yhprum" is "Murphy" spelled backwards.) The simple formula of Yhprum's law is: "Everything that can work, will work."

A more specific formulation of the law by [[Richard Zeckhauser]], a professor of [[political economy]] at [[Harvard University]], states: "Sometimes systems that should not work, work nevertheless."

Resnick ''et al''. (2006) used this law to describe how intensive and seemingly [[altruistic]] participation by giving ranking is observed in the [[eBay]] feedback system.<ref name=Resnick06>{{cite journal|last=Resnick|first=Paul|author2=Zeckhauser, Richard|author3=Swanson, John|author4=Lockwood, Kate|title=The value of reputation on eBay: A controlled experiment|journal=Experimental Economics|date=June 2006|volume=9|issue=2|pages=79–101|doi=10.1007/s10683-006-4309-2|url=http://www.hks.harvard.edu/fs/rzeckhau/postcards.pdf|archive-date=2009-12-13|access-date=2018-08-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091213162241/http://www.hks.harvard.edu/fs/rzeckhau/postcards.pdf|url-status=bot: unknown}}. Internet Archive  of 13.12.2009</ref>  Jøsang, in a discussion of online trust management, suggests that all similar "trust and reputation systems" are manifestations of Yhprum's law.  He states the law in a similar form to Zeckhauser: "Something that shouldn't work sometimes does work."<ref>Audun Jøsang, "Trust management in online communities", p. 87, ch. 4 in Volker Wittke and Heidemarie Hanekop (eds.), ''New Forms of Collaborative Innovation and Production on the Internet'', Universitätsverlag Göttingen, 2011 {{ISBN|9783863950200}}.</ref>  Arenas ''et al.'' in a similar discussion add the adjunct "...or at least work fairly well" to the law.<ref>Alvaro E. Arenas, Benjamin Aziz, Gheorghe Cosmin Silaghi, [https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/sec.146 "Reputation management in collaborative computing systems"], ''Security and Communication Networks'', vol. 3, iss. 6, pp. 546-564, November/December 2010.</ref>

==Origin==
Though Zeckhauser is often credited with coining, the first reference to Yhprum's law may have been by [[Alan Abelson]] in the financial newspaper [[Barron's (newspaper)|''Barron's'']] in December 1974.<ref>Robert W. Murphy, "New fiduciary responsibilities under the Pension Reform Act of 1974", ''Proceedings - Seminar on the Analysis of Security Prices'', vol. 20, iss. 1, pp. 73–112, [[Center for Research in Security Prices]], May 1975.</ref><ref>"News and Notes of AIChE", ''Chemical Engineering Progress'', vol. 71, iss. 4, April 1975</ref>  ''Barron's'' version of the law is more in the way of a corollary to Murphy's law than its opposite: "anything that should go wrong, won't".  Abelson coined the term to describe the gloomy financial predictions of the time which he thought were wrong, or at least wildly exaggerated.  In Abelson's opinion, a [[depression (economics)|depression]] only occurs when the warning signs are missed or ignored.  The very act of predicting one will ensure that it does not happen.<ref>Alan Abelson, "Up & down Wall Street", ''Barron's'' pp. 1, 27–28, 9 December 1974.</ref>
